gap.evidence: the need for enhanced catalyst durability and regeneration strategies
gap.reason: The introduction motivates improved automotive catalyst materials that maintain high activity under low-temperature and transient conditions, resist degradation over vehicle lifetimes, and reduce platinum-group-metal consumption.

broad.text: For automotive exhaust catalysts, what single intervention could improve catalytic activity and durability while reducing platinum-group-metal consumption? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

problem_constrained.text: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

expert_context.text: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

hidden_target.material_initial_state: Fresh 1 wt% multi-element alloy catalyst candidates prepared from up to 19 metal precursors and deposited on La-doped γ-Al2O3; the explored composition space ranged from five- to nineteen-element systems. Fresh catalysts commonly contained agglomerates of fine metallic particles and had not yet undergone accelerated thermal ageing.
hidden_target.intervention: A closed-loop, high-throughput discovery campaign coupled automated continuous-solvothermal synthesis, post-ageing activity screening, machine-learning prediction, Bayesian optimisation, and direct inverse analysis. In total, 1548 catalysts were synthesised and 1493 evaluated; elemental composition and synthesis parameters (200–350 °C, 20–35 MPa, precursor/reductant/25 M NaOH flow rates) were iteratively selected using post-ageing activity as the main design index.
hidden_target.conditions: Catalysts were aged at 900 °C for 5 h under cyclic lean/rich, water-containing gas, oxidised and reduced at 500 °C, and then tested from 100 to 500 °C at 10 °C min−1. The near-stoichiometric feed contained 500 ppm NO, 5000 ppm CO, 200 ppm C3H6, 120 ppm i-C5H12, 14% CO2, 4900 ppm O2, 1700 ppm H2, and N2 balance at 500 mL min−1. Performance indices included T50, T90, conversion at 350 °C, and total conversion over 150–450 °C.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: Post-ageing electronic and atomic reconstruction of multimetal sites, especially the emergence of electronically coupled Cu–Pt cooperative adsorption sites, together with process-dependent alloy/support interfacial states. Low synthesis temperature and high alkalinity favoured controlled multimetal reduction and limited detrimental phase segregation or incorporation of Fe/Ni/Cu into La–Al-based mixed oxides; simple particle size or sintering alone did not explain activity.
hidden_target.mechanism: Ageing can either activate or deactivate catalysts through element-specific electronic redistribution. Beneficial Cu–Pt surface rearrangement creates cooperative adsorption/activation sites, weakens overly strong CO binding, and improves redox buffering and oxygen mobility; by contrast, Pt coordination with Ni/Fe can electronically isolate Pt and suppress adsorption. During reaction, i-C5H12 oxidation consumes surface/gas-phase oxygen and generates locally reduced sites that enable NO reduction, coupling hydrocarbon oxidation to NO conversion. Sufficient alkalinity supports synchronous multimetal nucleation, while moderately low synthesis temperature limits coarsening and segregation.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to a Pd reference and to random exploration, inverse-model-guided selection of composition and processing—particularly noble-metal combinations enriched in Pd/Rh/Ga and a high-alkalinity, low-temperature synthesis window—was expected to yield more catalysts retaining superior low-temperature and total conversion after severe ageing.
hidden_target.baseline: A Pd/Al2O3 benchmark tested under identical post-ageing and multicomponent-feed conditions was the performance baseline; randomly selected catalyst compositions and synthesis conditions were the discovery-efficiency baseline. A hit required at least a 5 °C lower T50 or at least a 2 percentage-point improvement in conversion at 350 °C or total conversion relative to Pd.
hidden_target.boundary: The conclusions apply to the explored five- to nineteen-element, 1 wt% supported catalyst space under the specified accelerated ageing protocol and near-stoichiometric model exhaust containing NO, CO, C3H6, and i-C5H12. i-C5H12 served as a stringent redox probe rather than a complete representation of real exhaust. Detailed structure–performance assignments are based on selected ex situ examples, so a quantitative causal relation between nanoscale segregation and activity was not established.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: Automated light-off measurements of species-resolved NO, CO, C3H6, and i-C5H12 conversion, especially T50 and conversion at 350 °C after ageing, discriminated performance against Pd. Fresh-versus-aged CO-adsorption FT-IR tested changes in adsorption sites and electronic coupling, while HAADF-STEM/EDS assessed particle morphology, elemental distribution, and support-associated oxide phases. Predictive versus random hit rates were compared by 95% confidence intervals and Fisher’s exact test.
hidden_target.actual_result: Approximately 100 compositions surpassed Pd across relevant indices: 106 had ΔT50 ≤ −5 °C, 290 showed at least +2 percentage points in NO and i-C5H12 conversion at 350 °C, and 124 improved all four species by at least +2 percentage points over 150–450 °C. More than 99% of 508 fresh/aged pairs changed in at least one activity index. A beneficial example, hts0025, gained 52% NO and 75% i-C5H12 conversion at 350 °C and lowered their T50 values by 134 and 124 °C after ageing, coincident with newly observed Cu–CO and Pt–CO bands; a degrading catalyst lost its Pt–CO band despite no explanatory morphological difference. For matched-composition catalysts, high-alkali/245 °C synthesis improved 350 °C conversion by 64, 21, 28, and 73 percentage points for NO, CO, C3H6, and i-C5H12, respectively, relative to lower-alkali/264 °C synthesis. Predictive exploration achieved hit rates of 27.0%, 44.3%, and 37.2% for T50, 350 °C conversion, and overall conversion versus 1.3%, 3.1%, and 1.5% for random exploration—about 20–30-fold higher, with p < 0.001.
